transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-11-09
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 min
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Kim (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Novus - Head of ML), Samir Desai (Novus - Platform Eng), Priya Kapoor (Novus - CTO)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can see we have a full house, quick agenda: structured output demo, function/tool calling, guardrails and then q&a, sound good?
[00:18] Lena: yup great, thanks, we're mostly interested in reliable json outputs for product metadata extraction and safe tool calls into our inventory service.
[00:27] Jonah: cool, i'll kick off the demo in json mode, show schema enforcement and how Redwood's runtime enforces guardrails and function calling, note: some transcription may be off, so i'll try to be clear.

[02:05] Jonah: starting screen share — Redwood Console, route configured to use hosted inference cluster, model pinned to rdx-3b-v1-quant (demo model). first demo: structured output mode, we give a schema and ask for product json.
[02:37] Jonah: (typing) prompt: "Extract product: name, sku, price, category, availability: boolean, dimensions: {w,h,d} as numbers". schema attached via panel.
[03:12] Maya: quick note — json mode will validate against schema and if the model returns bad types we can auto-correct or reject based on policy.
[03:27] Samir: how strict is the correct vs reject behaviour? we have downstream ETL that breaks on malformed ints.
[03:36] Jonah: good question. policy levels: warn (return best-effort with warnings in metadata), coerce (try to cast types), and strict (reject and return error). you can set per-route. for production we'd recommend strict for important pipelines.

[05:00] Jonah: demo output (first call) - timestamp: 05:00 - model returned valid json, small diff in category naming ("mens-wear" vs our canonical "mens_clothing"), Console shows normalization rules mapping.
[05:28] Lena: does that mapping happen at runtime or postprocess?
[05:33] Jonah: runtime transform pipeline — you can attach small mapping functions or use builtin synonyms table. that's where function-calling helps.

[06:10] Jonah: next, function-calling demo: we define a tool - inventory.lookup(sku) which hits Novus inventory service. i'll simulate a call and show the tool result being injected back into the response.
[06:30] Jonah: invoke: model decides to call inventory.lookup with args {"sku":"NR-1873"}. Console shows call payload, then the runtime makes the outbound call (or can be routed to your VPC connector if private).
[07:02] Maya: important for security — outbound calls from hosted infra can be tunneled through customer VPC, and KMS keys can be used to decrypt any secrets.
[07:18] Priya: is that true for Dedicated as well? we have compliance constraints; can't have external egress except through our proxies.
[07:26] Jonah: Dedicated supports private-only egress and on-prem supports air-gapped. we map DNS and routes, and you can provide integration scripts.

[09:05] Samir: what's the latency when you do a function call and wait for a backend? we're worried about tokenization/roundtrip overhead.
[09:12] Jonah: good concern. typical extra latency is the backend call time; Redwood's runtime parallelizes IO where possible and returns partial streaming tokens while awaiting tool results if the model supports structured tool calling. for sync calls expect an added 100-400 ms for typical REST endpoints; can be more depending on your service.

[10:50] Jonah: switching to guardrails: we show policy rules in Console - regex checks on string fields, numeric ranges, allowlists/denylists for endpoints, and sensitive PII redaction. these are enforced pre-post model call in the runtime.
[11:25] Lena: can we enforce that price < 10000 or else reject?
[11:29] Jonah: yes, numeric range rule, we demoed that — if price out of range and strict mode is on, the call returns an error and the runtime logs the rejection with a reason in the trace.

[13:00] Jonah: now live demo: i'll deliberately craft a prompt that sometimes produces malformed dims (strings instead of numbers). demo route is set to coerce mode for this run.
[13:22] [13:22] Jonah: model result -> dimensions.width = "12.5" (string). runtime coerces to number 12.5 and adds a warning field in out.metadata.warnings. Console shows the event.
[13:48] Samir: where are those warnings accessible? we need them in Splunk.
[13:53] Jonah: Redwood's observability has export hooks; we can export traces, warnings, and per-token cost to your SIEM or to an S3 bucket.

[15:10] Maya: quick note on Optimize — it will recommend batching, quantization profile, and a model variant for your workload. for structured output you often can move to smaller quantized models with similar pass/fail rates which reduces cost.
[15:33] Priya: how do you measure pass/fail? we have strict accuracy targets for product extraction.
[15:37] Jonah: we run evals against your golden set; Redwood stores per-prompt evals and can alert regressions. Optimize suggests model/quantization that meets your success thresholds while lowering cost.

[17:50] Jonah: next part: function-calling guardrail examples. we set an allowlist of methods the model may call; block any calls that could mutate inventory without an explicit two-phase commit. also show rate limits on tool calls to protect backend.
[18:10] Lena: curious about retry semantics if your runtime fails the outbound call — do you retry? what about idempotency?
[18:16] Jonah: retries are configurable per-route; for non-idempotent calls we recommend no automatic retry and instead an explicit confirmation flow. Redwood supports idempotency tokens to help.

[20:00] Jonah: demo: model tries to call inventory.decrementStock(sku, qty). Because we have mutation-blocked policy the runtime returns a structured response asking to escalate to a confirmed action which triggers a manual approval step in the Console.
[20:22] Priya: nice, that fits our process.

[22:00] Jonah: switching to deeper technical notes — KV cache handling: for chat contexts we keep KV cache warm for pinned sessions, and in Dedicated you can have larger KV caches which reduces repeated tokenization. that helps with latency on repeated product lookups.
[22:42] Samir: does the KV cache include sensitive customer text? we need encryption at rest.
[22:47] Maya: yes, at rest encryption is supported and customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM are available for Private/Dedicated. plus audit logs for cache hits/misses.

[25:00] Jonah: back to schemas — when you provide a JSON schema we also show a per-field confidence score (model's confidence in each extracted field). you can use that to drive fallback rules.
[25:28] Lena: if confidence is low, can we route to a higher-capacity model automatically?
[25:33] Jonah: absolutely, Smart Routing rules can escalate to a higher tier or to a human review queue. you can set thresholds per-field or per-record.

[28:15] Maya: quick product note — for PII redaction we can mask on output and also prevent model from seeing certain fields by removing them from the prompt via a preprocessor.
[28:40] Priya: for compliance we need static redaction rules too, ideally pre-model.
[28:45] Jonah: supported. both pre and post processors available.

[31:00] Jonah: now i'll run a demo of a tool-chain: model extracts product json, calls inventory.lookup, then calls pricing.computeDiscount with customer tier, then returns a composed json. watch the Console trace: you can see model decision to call each function and the payloads.
[31:40] [31:40] Jonah: function calls are visible in the request trace with timings, token counts and cost.
[32:05] Samir: token cost visibility is important for our FinOps folks.
[32:10] Maya: Console shows per-route token breakdown, per-tool egress cost estimates, and Optimize suggestions to reduce tokens via batching and stricter stop sequences.

[34:20] Lena: one more security question: do you support SAML SSO + RBAC for the Console? we need fine-grained control for product teams.
[34:27] Maya: yes SAML + SCIM for provisioning, RBAC on per-route, and audit trails.

[36:10] Priya: latency targets — can Redwood guarantee p95 < 300ms for small requests?
[36:16] Jonah: for Dedicated with pinned GPUs and optimized kernels, p95 of single-token generation for small seqs is < 150ms in our benchmarks; with end-to-end including tool-calls it's workload dependent. SLA can be discussed in Dedicated contract.

[38:00] Samir: interested in pilot: we want to run a 1-week POC with 10k sample product pages, measure extraction accuracy, latency and cost.
[38:08] Maya: that's perfect — next steps: we'll send pilot pricing, Jonah will attach the benchmark checklist and we can schedule the POC kickoff.

[40:12] Maya: any final questions?
[40:18] Lena: only one — onboarding time for Dedicated? we have procurement windows.
[40:23] Maya: Dedicated typical lead time 4-8 weeks depending on capacity and network setup; Private on-prem longer. we can start Hosted pilot immediately.

[42:00] Recap:
- Demo covered JSON schema enforcement, coerce vs strict modes, per-field confidence, and normalization rules.
- Function/tool calling demo showed inventory.lookup and pricing.computeDiscount, plus allowlists and mutation-block policies.
- Guardrails: numeric ranges, regex checks, PII redaction, and rate limits.
- Security: SOC2, KMS/customer-managed keys, SAML + RBAC, VPC connectors for private egress.

[43:30] Next steps and action items reviewed (see action_items). Maya will send docs and pricing, Jonah will share benchmark checklist, Lena will provide sample prompts.

[44:10] Maya: great thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with links and the recording.

[44:18] Priya: thanks all, appreciate the thoroughness.

[44:22] Meeting ends.
